title: The Life You Want Won't Happen by Accident
author: Wisdom From Dad
summary: Starting from a morning surfing session that gets him dreaming about a winter surf trip, this father-focused newsletter builds an extended, deliberately absurd parable about the danger of taking action before defining what you actually want. The author imagines asking an AI for the nearest warm-water surf spot and getting Oregon instead of Mexico because he never specified that 'warm' meant warm, then connects the mistake to a real failure in his own life: leaving a successful executive career only to take, and quit, a post-retirement job that checked every box except the one that mattered — he didn't actually want to do the required work. The piece pivots to fatherhood specifically through Stephen Covey's 'begin with the end in mind' and the practice of 'bookending' the day (putting the most important commitments first, borrowed from Darren Hardy), arguing that a father's calendar is itself a silent lesson to his children, since 'your kids are watching how you allocate your time.' Its central claim for family life is that urgent things reliably crowd out important ones — a marriage or a child's need for attention never sends a formal request — so a father must schedule what matters before it becomes urgent, and that in doing so he is teaching his children how to build an intentional life by example, not instruction.
points: Uses a real career failure — leaving executive work for a job that 'checked all the boxes' but that he didn't actually want to do — to argue clear objectives must precede action.
Applies Stephen Covey's 'begin with the end in mind' and Darren Hardy's day-bookending practice specifically to fatherhood and family priorities.
Argues urgent demands (job, phone, house) reliably crowd out important ones (spouse, kids, health) because only the important ones stay silent until neglected.
Claims fathers teach children how to build an intentional life by example — 'your kids are watching how you allocate your time' — not by instruction.
Frames scheduling what matters before it becomes urgent as the practical discipline that prevents a life from 'happening by accident.'
quotes: If I had gone to Short Sands, in Oregon, I would not have gotten what I wanted. My seemingly perfect plan would produce the wrong result simply because my objective wasn’t clear. I had no desire to be COLD.
I was capable of doing these things, but my WHY wasn’t big enough to keep me engaged in work I truly didn’t care for. The truth is, I didn’t want to surf in cold water.
Before you take that first step in your 1,000-mile journey, make sure you’re headed toward something you really want - and that you’re willing and able to do what’s necessary to get there.

Your kids won’t send you a meeting request that says, “Dad, I’m going to need you to pay attention to me sometime in the next six months.” Your marriage doesn’t send you a reminder when your spouse needs attention.
You are developing leaders whether you realize it or not. Your kids are watching how you allocate your time, and they see what gets your attention.
You’re not just planning the days and weeks of your life. You’re teaching your children how to plan theirs.
If you don’t schedule the important things, the urgent things will gladly take their place.
